entries.note: Descriptions of mechanism of English credit institutions, with able discussions of many points of theory.
Shows that tendency to substitute credit in place of material substances is the distinctive mark of progress in the art of effecting exchange.

Contents: Three centuries of cheap money in the United States; Paper currency of North Carolina; Paper currency of New Hampshire. Bibliography, p. 275–88. General thesis: Inflationist movement always due to scarcity of capital in sparsely settled regions.
entries.noteSource: D. R. Dewey in Amer. hist. r. 6: 579.

entries.note: Bibliography by Hugh Williams, p. 347–77. Defines terms, discusses indications, accompanying conditions, causes and preventives; brief history of crises and depressions in United States. Diagrams, index.
What funds are, how obtained and how operated through U. S. treasury, savings and commercial banks, building associations, brokerage, trust and insurance companies. Facsimiles of business paper.
List of authorities, p. 577–81.
Mainly a balancing of arguments. No one book will give an intelligent reader a better grasp of the controversy.
Succinct account of fundamental character of banking operations, nature of credit and its practical manifestation in the chief forms, checks and banknotes.
Partial list of authorities, p. 429–32. No one else has been so successful in obtaining useful information on this subject within the limits proposed.

Bibliography, p. 435–99. 1776–1860, coinage system, paper currency; 1861–90, U. S. legal tender notes, silver question, national banking system; 1891–1902, silver contest of 1896, reform act of 1900. General review, bibliography. U. S. laws and other documents in appendix.
Elementary. Contains descriptions of clearinghouse and check bank. Excellent for laying a basis of sound doctrines.
Special emphasis on constitutionality of government paper money. Historical rather than controversial; not exhaustive, but adequate.
By a monometalist. Serviceable historical compendium, if reader bears in mind that author writes to persuade.
Bibliographies. Comprehensive treatment. First of a proposed series of 6 volumes on money and banking.
List of references, p. 353–63. Intended for college use and as handbook for average citizen. On points at issue all important views are set forth clearly. Bibliographic references.
entries.noteSource: H. A. Mills in Annals Amer. acad. pol. sci. 22: 126.

entries.note: Reviews briefly history of gold and silver currency and argues strongly for international bimetallism. Opposes free coinage of silver.
States and impartially examines various theories. Holds that paper money nominally or really convertible into coin is liable to overissue.
First published in 1879. An abridgment of Money, with added chapters.
History of gold and silver coinage in U. S. beginning with Massachusetts colonial mint, 1652. Opposes free coinage of silver.
Bibliographies. Treats evolution of money, the gold standard, fiat money as developed in colonial, continental and federal currency, and banks.
Accurate, noncontroversial record of facts, by a tariff reformer. For general students.
